sentences.text: 1. Vide this order, this court shall adjudicate the present criminal appeal whereby the appellant has assailed the impugned judgment and order on sentence dated 08.11.2017 and 29.11.2017 respectively, passed by Ld. MM/SED, whereby the appellant was convicted to simple imprisonment for a period of 6 months for the offence u/s 304A IPC and sentenced to undergo simple imprisonment for a period of one month for the offence punishable u/s 279 IPC.
IMPUGNED ORDER FACTS 2.

The facts of the case are hereby succinctly recapitulated: It was alleged that on 23.11.2006, at about 09:50 PM near DCD Toll Road near Picket no.4 one truck make Tata 407 was being driven on the wrong side of the road from Noida side.
Ct Shakeel who was on beat duty spotted the truck signaled it to stop.
It was further alleged that the driver did not stop the vehicle and collided with a car and the car caught fire due to its impact.
Constable noticed the number of Tata 407 vehicle as DL-1LD-1274.
The driver of the truck tried to escape but was caught by Ct. Shakil.

His identity was discovered as Bir Bahadur s/o Ram Singh, r/o village Babadm PS Churki, District Jalon, Jhansi,
Uttar Pradesh.
It was further alleged that both the vehicles got engulfed in flames.
The driver of the car got burnt alive inside the vehicle ass he could not come out.
In the meanwhile, fire brigade came to the spot to douse the fire.
On the complaint of Ct Shakil, a rukka was prepared.
It was also alleged that the injured/driver of the car succumbed to his injuries and was reported as dead.
Thus, the present FIR u/s 279/304A IPC got registered.

sentences.text: After weighing the evidence, the Ld Trial Court opined that driving a truck on the wrong side of the road in the night is an act which is rash.
Ld. Trial Court further held that the accused was driving in a negligent manner.
Thus, Ld Trial Court convicted the appellant for the offences punishable u/s 279/304A IPC.
CONTENTIONS OF LD. COUNSELS FOR THE APPELLANT &THE RESPONDENT 4.
Ld. LAC for the appellant submitted that the presence of eye witness HC Shakil is highly doubtful.

Ld. LAC invited the Court's attention to the cross-examination of PW1 HC Shakil dated 09.05.2016,
in order to contend that HC Shakil did not even remember the DD entry by which he left the PS for his patrolling duty neither had he remembered the exact time when he left for patrolling.

Ld. LAC for appellant contended that even in the cross-examination of PW-7 dated 15.03.2017, Inspector Heeralal submitted that he had not filed any copy of Roznamcha register regarding patrolling duty of HC Shakil on record.
5. Thus, Ld. LAC for appellant submitted that apart from this witness there is no other public witness who joined the investigation or could prove the case of prosecution beyond reasonable doubt.
6. Ld. LAC for appellant further submitted that it was Shivbala who drove the vehicle in question and not accused/appellant herein.

To substantiate his contention,, Ld. LAC further invited the Court's attention to examination in chief of PW-5 dated 30.05.2013, to contend that PW-5 deposed that his driver namely Shivbala was engaged was driver to drive the vehicle in question.
7. Per contra, Ld. Addl. PP for State/ respondent submitted that there was no previous enmity or any such motive for the complainant to falsely implicate the accused/appellant herein.
Ld. Addl PP for State further contended that complainant HC Shakil is an independent witness and his presence at the spot is natural as he was posted at PS NFC, at the relevant time.
It was further submitted that the defense of Shivbala driving the vehicle in question cannot be countenanced in view of the fact that the accused was apprehended at the spot only.
8. Submissions heard.
DECISION IDENTITY OF ACCUSED 9.

As far as identity of appellant/convict being the driver of truck in question is concerned, it had been categorically averred by eye witness HC Shakil Ahmad that on 23.11.2006, when he was on patrolling duty , he reached at DND Toll road at about 09:50 PM and he witnessed the accident.

He specifically stated as thus:
"The driver of the offending vehicle tried to run away and I apprehended him."
10.
It has also come in the testimony of the witness that the IO arrested the convict/appellant vide Ex. PW1/F.

The IO also seized the driving license of the convict/appellant vide seizure memo Ex.
Veer Bahadur Singh vs State (Government Of Nct Of Delhi) on 17 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/129382955/
2 PW1/E, and also carried out personal search of the accused vide Ex. PW1/G.

entities.text: Veer Bahadur Singh vs State (Government Of Nct Of Delhi)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The identity of offending vehicle was not disputed by the appellant/convict.
11.Thus, this witness identified the accused as being the driver of the vehicle in question.
He had proved his complaint as Ex. PW1/A and his testimony before the Court corroborated his version given in the complaint.
A plea was put forth by the Ld. LAC for convict that it was not the appellant herein who was driving the vehicle but it was one Shivbala who was driving the said vehicle.
However, this suggestion was denied by PW-1 HC Shakil.

Even PW-5 Prahalad Pal registered owner of the truck in question DL1LD1274 avowed that his brother Shivbala used the vehicle, however,
denied the suggestion that Shivbala was driving the vehicle on the day of the incident.
12. False implication of appellant is also ruled out, in view of the fact that rukka Ex. PW7/A reveals that the date of incident 23.11.2006 and the time of the incident was around 09:45 PM.
In this very complaint, the factum of accused/convict being Veer Bahadur Singh has been cogently established.
Thus, the name of the appellant/convict finds mentioned at the very first instance.
This fact of apprehension was corroborated by PW- 1 when he stepped in the witness box.
Ld. Trial Court has correctly inferred that the testimony of PW-1 Shakil qua the identity of driver remained unrebutted and therefore there ought to be no reason to not rely upon the same.
13.Significantly, the appellant/convict did not dispute his presence at the spot.
Whilst recording his statement u/s 313 Cr.PC he merely replied in a bland 'it is incorrect'.
The appellant did not even put forth a plausible plea of alibi and merely blamed the police for falsely implicating him.
The arrest memo and other documents coupled with the factum of appellant being apprehended at the spot clearly establishes the identity of the appellant as being the driver of the offending vehicles.
INJURIES CAUSED AND CONSEQUENT DEATH 14.

It was vividly deposed by PW-1 HC Shakil that the truck in question Tata no 407 bearing no DL11LD1274 had collided with the Maruti esteemed car head, on which resultantly led to the esteem car catching fire.
The postmortem report of the victim reflects that the victim suffered 100% burnt injuries which ultimately resulted in death.
In this context PW-6 BL Chaudhary, Department of Forensic Medicine Lady Harding Medical College, New Delhi, deposed the he conducted the postmortem on dead body of Jitender s/o Shyam Lal.

entities.text: Department of Forensic Medicine Lady Harding Medical College, New Delhi
entities.label: ORG

sentences.text:
He proved the postmortem report as Ex.
PW6/A and opined that the cause of death was shock due to 100% deep burns, which were antemortem in nature.
This fact also lends credence to the versions of prosecution qua the factum of death caused due to burning of vehicles upon their collision.
15.As far as identity of the deceased is concerned
, PW-3 Mahipal Singh brought to the fore that he was registered owner of Maruti Car bearing no HR51D6371 and he had appointed the deceased Jitender as driver of the said Car.
He had further deposed that on the day of the incident ie on 23.11.2006, the driver Jitender had gone to Noida to meet his sister.
PW- 3 categorically deposed that he had gone to AIIMS Hospital and he identified the dead body of Jitender.
No suggestion was given to any of the witnesses that the collision between the Truck and the Car had not taken place.

Thus, the factum of death of the deceased due to accident has been cogently established by the Veer Bahadur Singh vs State (Government Of Nct Of Delhi) on 17 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/129382955/
3 prosecution.
RASHNESS AND NEGLIGENCE 16.Once the factum of appellant driving the impugned vehicle in question and the factum of death of the victim Jitender had been established, the moot question remains whether the convict was driving the vehicle in rash and negligent manner.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: At this juncture, it would be apposite to peruse the following extracts of Ravi Kapur Vs State of Rajasthan Criminal Appeal No.1838 Of 2009 which elucidate the law on rashness and negligence "12Rash and negligent driving has to be examined in light of the facts and circumstances of a given case.

entities.text: Ravi Kapur Vs State of Rajasthan Criminal Appeal No.1838 Of 2009
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is a fact incapable of being construed or seen in isolation.
It must be examined in light of the attendant circumstances.
A person who drives a vehicle on the road is liable to be held responsible for the act as well as for the result.
It may not be always possible to determine with reference to the speed of a vehicle whether a person was driving rashly and negligently.
Both these acts presuppose an abnormal conduct.
Even when one is driving a vehicle at a slow speed but recklessly and negligently, it would amount to 'rash and negligent driving' within the meaning of the language of Section 279 IPC.
That is why the legislature in its wisdom has used the words 'manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life'.

The preliminary conditions, thus, are that (a) it is the manner in which the vehicle is driven; (b) it be driven either rashly or negligently; and (c) such rash or negligent driving should be such as to endanger human life.
Once these ingredients are satisfied, the penalty contemplated under Section 279 IPC is attracted."

"13'Negligence' means omission to do something which a reasonable and prudent person guided by the considerations which ordinarily regulate human affairs would do or doing something which a prudent and reasonable person guided by similar considerations would not do.

Negligence is not an absolute term but is a relative one;
it is rather a comparative term.
It is difficult to state with precision any mathematically exact formula by which negligence or lack of it can be infallibly measured in a given case.

Whether there exists negligence per se or the course of conduct amounts to negligence will normally depend upon the attending and surrounding facts and circumstances which have to be taken into consideration by the Court.
In a given case, even not doing what one was ought to do can constitute negligence."
"14 The Court has to adopt another parameter, i.e., 'reasonable care' in determining the question of negligence or contributory negligence.

The doctrine of reasonable care imposes an obligation or a duty upon a person (for example a driver) to care for the pedestrian on the road and this duty attains a higher degree when the pedestrian happen to be children of tender years.

It is axiomatic to say that while driving a vehicle on a public way, there is an implicit duty cast on the drivers to see that their driving does not endanger the life of the right users of the road, may be either vehicular users or pedestrians.
They are expected to take sufficient care to avoid danger to others"

4 17.In the present matter
, in order to establish whether there was rashness or negligence on the part of the appellant, it would be apt to reproduce the following testimony of eye witness PW-1 HC Shakil.
"On 23.11.2006, I was posted as Constable at PS NFC.
On that day I was on patrolling duty on motorcycle bearing no. DL1SM0542 in the area of PS NFC.
At about 09:50 PM, I reached at DCD Toll Road Picket no. 4 through Ashram side.
I saw one TATA 407 bearing no DL11LD1274 was coming from Ashram side and going towards Noida side in wrong side.

I signaled the driver present in the Court today of the vehicle to stop but he did not stop his vehicle and he was driving the vehicle inn a rash and negligent manner and hit a maruti esteem car due to the collusion, fire broke out in both the vehicles.
The driver of the offending vehicle tried to ran away and I apprehended him.
The esteem car was totally inflamed and the driver of the esteem car was also burnt."
18.As is explicit from the above testimony, the impugned truck was not only being driven in a rash and negligent manner but also was going on the wrong side.
Mere driving on the wrong side of the road itself, speaks volumes of the culpability of the appellant/convict.
It is a case where the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur i.e. things speak for itself, is attracted.
In Ravi Kapoor (supra) it was held as "
15The other principle that is pressed in aid by the courts in such cases is the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur.

This doctrine serves two purposes - one that an accident may by its nature be more consistent with its being caused by negligence for which the opposite party is responsible than by any other causes and that in such a case, the mere fact of the accident is prima facie evidence of such negligence.
Secondly, it is to avoid hardship in cases where the claimant is able to prove the accident but cannot prove how the accident occurred.
The courts have also applied the principle of res ipsa loquitur in cases where no direct evidence was brought on record.
The Act itself contains a provision which concerns with the consequences of driving dangerously alike the provision in the IPC that the vehicle is driven in a manner dangerous to public life.
Where a person does such an offence he is punished as per the provisions of Section 184 of the Act.
The courts have also taken the concept of 'culpable rashness' and 'culpable negligence' into consideration in cases of road accidents.

'Culpable rashness' is acting with the consciousness that mischievous and illegal consequences may follow but with the hope that they will not and often with the belief that the actor has taken sufficient precautions to prevent their happening.
The imputability arises from acting despite consciousness (luxuria).

'Culpable negligence' is acting without the consciousness that the illegal and mischievous effect will follow, but in circumstances which show that the actor has not exercised the caution incumbent upon him and that if he had, he would have had the consciousness.
The imputability arises from the neglect of civic duty of circumspection.
In such a case the mere fact of accident is prima facie evidence of such negligence.

This maxim suggests that on the circumstances of a given case the res speaks and is eloquent because the facts stand unexplained, with the result that the natural and reasonable inference from the facts, not a conjectural inference, shows that the act is attributable to some person's negligent conduct.
[Ref. Justice Rajesh Tandon's 'An Exhaustive Commentary on Motor Vehicles Act, 1988"

sentences.text: "16 We have noticed these principles in order to examine the questions raised in the present case in their correct perspective.
We may notice that certain doctrines falling in the realm of accidental civil or tortuous jurisprudence, are quite applicable to the cases falling under criminal jurisprudence like the present one."

19.As is apparent from the testimony of PW-1 which remained unconverted, PW-1 had signaled the driver to stop the vehicle but the convict driver continued to drive the vehicle, and as a result collided head on with the vehicle of the deceased.
The rashness, by driving on the wrong side, is writ large from the facts and circumstances of the case.

And as rightly observed by the Ld. Trial Court,
continued driving of the vehicle indicates towards gross negligence on part of the convict/driver.
CONCLUSION 20.

Ergo, in view of the aforesaid discussion, this Court finds no infirmity in the impugned judgment and order on sentence dated 08.11.2017 and 29.11.2017 respectively, passed by Ld. MM, South-East,
Saket Courts, New Delhi, and thus the present Criminal Appeal qua the judgment of the trial Court,
filed by the appellant, is hereby dismissed.
21.Arguments on quantum of sentence also heard.

Counsel for appellant/convict remonstrated that the order on sentence dated 29.11.2017 passed by Ld. Trial Court be set aside, inasmuch as the order whereby the convict was sentenced to simple imprisonment for 6 month is too harsh.
It was also submitted that the convict/appellant may be let off on probation as he is first time offender and is sole bread earner of his family and comes from very poor background.
23. Per contra, Ld. Addl PP for State/respondent submitted that the convict/appellant does not deserve leniency as he is a professional driver.
24.Submissions of Ld. Counsel for appellant heard.
However, this Court finds no infirmity in the order on sentence dated 29.11.2017 passed by Ld. Trial Court.
The Ld Trial Court has elaborately dealt with the aspect of sentencing, and this Court concurs with its reasoning.

Thus, the order on sentence dated passed by Ld Trial Court is hereby upheld and appellant herein is sentenced to undergo simple imprisonment for six months for the offence punishable u/s 304A IPC and one month simple imprisonment for offence u/s 279 IPC.
Both the sentences shall run concurrently.

25.Copy of this order be sent to Ld. Secretary DLSA/SED, Saket with a request to disburse adequate compensation to the next of kin ie family members of the deceased, under the Delhi Victim Compensation Scheme, 2018.

26.TCR, if any, alongwith copy of this order be sent to Ld. Trial Court for necessary information/
compliance.
27.Appeal file be consigned to record room after due compliance.
